title: Generative AI vs Predictive AI
objectives: Define predictive (discriminative) AI and generative AI and state the core difference.
Explain the difference in terms of what each model learns: P(y|x) versus P(x) or P(x, y).
Compare outputs, evaluation methods, data needs and risks of both approaches.
Decide which approach suits a given business problem, or how to combine them.
Recognise hybrid systems where a predictive model and a generative model work together.
definition: Predictive AI uses historical data to estimate an outcome for a new input, such as a class label, a probability or a number: 'Will this customer churn?'. Generative AI learns the patterns of the data itself so it can produce new content, such as text, images or code: 'Write a retention email to this customer.' Predictive models answer questions about data; generative models create data.

theory.heading: What each approach learns
theory.body: In probability terms, a predictive (discriminative) model learns the conditional probability P(y | x): given an input x, how likely is each label y? It focuses only on the boundary between classes. A generative model learns how the data is distributed, P(x) or the joint P(x, y), so it can sample new x that look like the training data. A large language model learns P(next token | previous tokens) and generates text by sampling from that distribution one token at a time.
points: Predictive: learns decision boundaries, outputs a label, score or number.
Generative: learns the data distribution, outputs new samples (sentences, images, audio).
An LLM is technically trained with a predictive objective (next-token prediction) but used generatively, by chaining predictions.

theory.heading: Output, evaluation and correctness
theory.body: Predictive outputs are usually checkable against a known answer, so they are evaluated with metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC or RMSE on a labelled test set. Generative outputs are open-ended: many different summaries can be correct. They are evaluated with human review, rubric-based LLM-as-judge scoring, reference-overlap metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) or task success rates. This difference shapes how you test and monitor each system in production.
points: Predictive: one correct answer per input; objective metrics.
Generative: many acceptable answers; quality, faithfulness and safety must be judged.
Generative outputs can be fluent but wrong (hallucinations), which predictive models do not produce in the same way.

theory.heading: Data, cost and explainability
theory.body: Predictive models are often trained on a company's own labelled, structured data and can be small, cheap and explainable (feature importance, SHAP values). Generative foundation models are pre-trained on huge unlabelled corpora by a few providers, then adapted by prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning. They are expensive to run per request and harder to explain. In regulated domains such as lending or insurance, the explainability of predictive models is often a legal requirement.
points: Predictive: labelled task-specific data, low inference cost, easier to audit.
Generative: massive pre-training, higher per-request cost, harder to audit.
Generative models can create synthetic training data to help predictive models when labels are scarce.

theory.heading: Combining both in one product
theory.body: Most real products use both. An e-commerce site predicts which products a user will buy (predictive recommendation) and then writes a personalised product description or email (generative). A support desk classifies a ticket's urgency (predictive) and drafts a reply (generative). A useful interview framing is: predictive AI decides or ranks, generative AI communicates or creates.
points: Fraud: predictive model scores the transaction; LLM writes the analyst summary.
HR: predictive model screens attrition risk; LLM drafts the stay-interview questions.
Routing a request to the right model is itself often a predictive step.

example.title: Same customer, two questions
example.body: A telecom company holds a customer's usage history. A predictive model, for example logistic regression, outputs a churn probability of 0.82. Because the probability is high, the system asks a generative model to write a friendly retention offer. The predictive model chose who to contact; the generative model chose what to say. The code shows the shape of both calls.

code.source:
# Predictive step: a trained classifier returns a probability
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X = [[2, 1], [30, 0], [5, 1], [25, 0]]   # [months_active, complaints_last_month]
y = [1, 0, 1, 0]                          # 1 = churned
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
risk = clf.predict_proba([[3, 1]])[0][1]
print(f'churn risk: {risk:.2f}')          # a high probability, e.g. 0.8+

# Generative step: only if risk is high, build a prompt for an LLM
if risk > 0.7:
    prompt = ('Write a short, friendly SMS offering a 20% discount to a customer '
              'who joined 3 months ago and complained last month.')
    print(prompt)  # send this to any LLM API; the reply text varies per run

use_cases.title: Predictive: credit and fraud
use_cases.description: Credit scoring, transaction fraud detection and insurance claim risk, where decisions must be accurate and explainable.

use_cases.title: Predictive: forecasting
use_cases.description: Demand forecasting, inventory planning, predictive maintenance and price estimation.

use_cases.title: Generative: content and communication
use_cases.description: Emails, reports, product descriptions, chat replies and meeting summaries.

use_cases.title: Generative: software and design
use_cases.description: Code generation, test creation, UI mock-ups and image or video assets.

use_cases.title: Hybrid: customer support
use_cases.description: Classify ticket priority and sentiment, then generate a draft reply grounded in the knowledge base.

demonstration.description: Feed one product review to both kinds of model. The predictive model returns a fixed label and a confidence; the generative model returns new text. Running the generative prompt again can give different wording, while the classifier returns the same score every time.

code.source:
Review: "Battery dies in 3 hours and support never replied."

Predictive model (sentiment classifier) -> label + probability
Generative model prompt -> "Write a polite reply apologising and offering a replacement."

demonstration.output:
Classifier: negative (0.97)
LLM: "We're sorry about the battery issue and the delay in our response. We'd like to send you a replacement right away..." (wording varies)

takeaways: Predictive AI estimates an outcome (label, probability, number); generative AI creates new content.
Predictive models learn P(y|x); generative models learn the data distribution P(x) or P(x, y).
Predictive outputs have one correct answer and objective metrics; generative outputs need quality and faithfulness evaluation.
Predictive models are usually cheaper and easier to explain, which matters in regulated decisions.
Most products combine both: predictive to decide, generative to communicate.

interview.question: What is the difference between generative and predictive AI?
interview.answer: Predictive AI estimates an outcome for an input, such as a class or a number. Generative AI creates new content, such as text or images, by learning the patterns of the training data.
interview.explanation: Give one example each (fraud scoring vs drafting an email). Strong answers also mention the output type: a label or score versus open-ended content.

interview.question: Explain discriminative vs generative models in probability terms.
interview.answer: A discriminative model learns P(y|x), the probability of a label given the input. A generative model learns P(x) or P(x, y), the distribution of the data, so it can sample new inputs.
interview.explanation: Classic examples: logistic regression is discriminative; Naive Bayes is generative. Interviewers like this precise framing for ML roles.

interview.question: An LLM is trained to predict the next token. Is it predictive or generative?
interview.answer: Its training objective is a prediction (the next-token distribution), but by repeatedly sampling a token and feeding it back it generates new sequences, so it is used as a generative model.
interview.explanation: This catches candidates who think the two are completely separate. The key idea is autoregressive generation built from repeated prediction.

interview.question: How would you evaluate a churn model versus a summarisation model?
interview.answer: The churn model is evaluated on labelled data with precision, recall, F1 or AUC. The summariser needs human or LLM-as-judge ratings for faithfulness, coverage and fluency, optionally with ROUGE against reference summaries.
interview.explanation: Shows that evaluation strategy depends on whether the output has a single correct answer, a frequent production concern.

interview.question: When should you NOT use generative AI?
interview.answer: When the task is a structured decision with a single correct answer, needs strict explainability or very low latency and cost, or when errors are unacceptable without review. A predictive model or rules is usually safer there.
interview.explanation: Interviewers value judgement over hype. Mention cost, determinism, explainability and hallucination risk.

practice.title: Route tasks to predictive or generative AI
practice.objective: Practise recognising whether a task asks for a decision or estimate (predictive) or for new content (generative), the first design choice in any AI project.
practice.statement: Read task descriptions and classify each one by its verbs. Split the text into words (lowercase, letters only; treat any non-letter as a separator). Generative verbs: write, draft, generate, summarize, summarise, translate, compose, rewrite, create. Predictive verbs: classify, predict, detect, forecast, estimate, score, flag, rank. If a task contains verbs from both lists, it is hybrid; from only one list, it is generative or predictive; from neither, it is unclear. Finally print how many tasks fell into each class.
practice.input_format: First line: N. Next N lines: one task description each.
practice.output_format:
For each task: . where index starts at 1 and class is generative, predictive, hybrid or unclear. Then: generative= predictive=

hybrid= unclear=

example.input:
3
Predict which customers will churn next month
Write a welcome email for new users
Detect fraud and draft an alert message for the analyst
example.output:
1. predictive
2. generative
3. hybrid
generative=1 predictive=1 hybrid=1 unclear=0

constraints: Matching is on whole words only: 'scored' does not match 'score'.
explanation: Lowercase the line and extract runs of letters with a regular expression, so punctuation and digits act as separators.
Put the words in a set and intersect it with each verb set; a non-empty intersection means that kind of verb is present.
Both present means hybrid, one present decides the class, none means unclear.
Keep a counter per class and print the summary in a fixed order.

tests.input:
3
Predict which customers will churn next month

generative=1 predictive=1 hybrid=1 unclear=0

generative=1 predictive=0 hybrid=1 unclear=0

quiz.question: A discriminative (predictive) classifier primarily learns which quantity?
options: A random sample of training data
P(y | x), the label given the input
quiz.explanation: Discriminative models learn the conditional probability of the label given the input, i.e. the decision boundary.

quiz.question: An insurer must decide whether to approve claims and explain each decision to a regulator. Which approach is the most suitable core?
options: An explainable predictive model, with GenAI only for drafting letters
A generative model that writes the decision freely
quiz.explanation: The decision is a structured, regulated prediction that needs explainability; generative AI can help communicate it.

quiz.question: Why is evaluating a summarisation model harder than evaluating a spam classifier?
options: Spam classifiers have no test data
Many different summaries can be correct, so there is no single right answer
Summaries cannot be read by humans
quiz.explanation: Open-ended outputs need judgement on faithfulness and quality, while a classifier is compared with one correct label.

quiz.question: A retailer predicts which users will buy running shoes, then sends each a personalised message written by an LLM. What kind of system is this?
options: Hybrid: predictive targeting plus generative content
quiz.explanation: The targeting is a prediction and the message is generated content, so the system combines both approaches.

quiz.question: Which risk is specific to generative models rather than predictive classifiers?
quiz.explanation: Hallucination, confident invented content, arises because generative models produce open-ended outputs.
